CONGRANT.TITLE: Collaborative Effort to Enhance Water Supply for Agriculture and Food Development through Educational Training of Hispanic Professionals
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Currently, there is limited representation of Hispanic in FANH sciences due to limited resources available to recruit and retain them in programs leading to careers in this area. The main purpose of this effort will be to attract and recruit Hispanic students into FANH and related sciences through exemplary outreach activities, K-12 summer experiences, summer internships, and social events. In order to retain the Hispanic students in the FANH sciences disciplines, we will utilize interactive class and lab modules, research-based hands-on experiences, mentoring, student led organization events, professional training sessions, and financial support in the form of research assistantships. The research will focus on water management among various sectors which include food, agriculture, and natural resource development. The research will enable students to interact and learn from professionals in the various sectors of FANH sciences, while also gaining the required knowledge to develop innovative methods that enhance water resource management. These efforts will directly support 64 high school students in summer enrichment camps, 16 undergraduate students through research-based experiences, 6 students through summer internships at USDA agencies, and 2 graduate students with research assistantship. Overall, the program will impact over 8,000 K-12 students through outreach activities and summer camps with over 1,000 undergraduate students in Engineering and Science through designated courses, technical talks, and other professional and social events. We plan to increase the number of students pursuing careers and research positions in FANH sciences through career guidance workshops, internship experiences, and graduate program scholarships. The RGV area is known for its rich agriculture history (sugar cane, citrus orchards and cattle ranching) and economy, and serves as a wonderful setting for promoting FANH sciences among Hispanic.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Texas Sea Grant College Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
- Preproposal submitted -

The proposed project is to develop electrically conductive concrete pipes to remove soluble cationic contaminants from run-off water via electrochemical precipitation and to protect Texas water resources including the ocean water. Concrete pipes can become conductive with added graphite and precipitate soluble cations by binding with carbonate or hydroxide at the elevated pH around the cathodic conductive concrete pipes. Metallic anodes will be used in combination. The research team will look at the removal of water hardness and heavy metals (e.g., lead, chromium-6) by the proposed novel technology. Previous research at the PI’s lab has shown that the concrete block with graphite additives as a cathode can remove 20-30% of water hardness with titanium as an anode (Billah and Kim, 2020). This study needs to be expanded to gauge the applicability to treat contaminated run-off water thus protecting Texas natural water resources including the Gulf of Mexico. The specific objectives of the project are to:

1) Determine the optimum operational conditions (voltage, ampere, graphite contents, the distance between electrodes, etc.) of the electrically conductive concrete for the most efficient hardness removal.
2) Check if the electrically conductive concrete pipes can be used to remove hardness from the tap water under both batch and continuous flow conditions. Also, focuses will be given to changes in the concentration of chlorine disinfectant and acidity of tap water.
3) Check if other soluble heavy metals in the tap water can be removed from the electrically conductive concrete pipe operated under optimum conditions that will be determined from Task 1.
4) Provide the preliminary version of construction, installation, and operational/maintenance guidance.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification desalination
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: A novel process to desalinate seawater is to be developed through the proposed work. Specifically, an ocean-based and nature-powered humidification-dehumidification (HDH) desalination process will be demonstrated in a lab scale. Innovative approaches include: (i) a floating system directly situated in the coastal water with no seawater intake and no brine discharge, (ii) a fully nature-powered mechanism directly driven by multiple renewable energy sources with zero usage of electricity, and (iii) a unique humidifier design using cloth wetting and wave overtopping to enhance mass transfer. The enabled desalination plant will be simple, robust, and environmentally-friendly, and is expected to produce freshwater in both large and small scales cost-effectively to meet diverse needs. Water quality analysis will be conducted in parallel with the technological advancement. The requested funds will be used to cover expenses on: wages for three graduate research assistants, summer salaries for three faculty members (the applicants), materials and supplies for the lab-scale prototype construction and water quality analysis, small instruments for testing the prototype, travel fees, and indirect costs. The proposed project will contribute to accomplishing the objectives 1, 2, 4, 5 defined in Water Desalination Act of 1996 as amended by WIIN Act and the objective 5 defined in Desalination 2008, as listed in page 2 of the FOA.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Biochar-Geomedia Water Filter for the Colonias, South Texas
CONGRANT.SPONORG: EPA Annual P3 Awards: A National Student Design Competition Focusing on People, Prosperity and the Planet
CONGRANT.OTHER_AGENCIES: Along the U.S.-Mexico border, about 400,000 low-income, immigrant Latinos have settled in Colonias in Texas – residential subdivisions, usually low-lying areas of a county, lacking the basic services such as water and sewer, paved roads, electricity, and drainage. The colonia households near Donna Canal and Reservoir (Superfund site) in Hidalgo County, Texas, have concerns about their tap water quality due to elevated level of lead and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB). Thus, colonia residents often rely on bottled water and water mill, resulting in an economic burden to the communities. The proposed project is designed to address basic sanitation and drinking water for homes in disadvantaged communities - Safe and Sustainable Water Resources. To this end, the project team will develop a prototype of point-of-use treatment system as a pour-through filter. The goal of project is to develop a low-cost filter made of locally-sourced biomass and geomaterial (pumice) in mixed-media, benefiting the colonia communities as an alternative to expensive commercial water filter systems.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Electrochemical precipitation of tap water from Lower Rio Grande Valley area with conductive concrete pipes.
CONGRANT.SPONORG: EPA Annual P3 Awards: A National Student Design Competition Focusing on People, Prosperity and the Planet
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Objective: Tap water in LRGV is extremely hard with more than 350 mg/L as CaCO3. Also, there have been reports about heavy metals in drinking water in rural communities in Lower Rio Grande Valley (LRGV) area. Thus, residents in the region depended on bottled water and watermill for drinking water, which has imposed an economical burden on them. More so is witnessed from the economically depressed area like Colonias. The proposed project is designed to remove soluble cations like water hardness and heavy metals from the tap water to ensure economical, safe, and sustainable water resources to all the local municipalities in the LRGV area. The project team proposes to develop a novel in-situ electrochemical precipitation (EP) using conductive concrete pipes as a cathode and a metallic anode. If combined with solar power, the proposed technology will be an eco-friendly water softening and cleaning system with minimum maintenance.
Description: The proposed P3 project will focus on developing a novel in-situ EP technology to remove soluble metallic contaminants from drinking water. It involves using conductive concrete as a cathode and a metallic anode in a batch or continuous flow condition. The research team in this proposal have been investigating water hardness removal using conductive concrete and metallic anode subjected to a range of power input. Previous project results from the PI’s lab showed 30% hardness removal at 15 V for 1 hr. trial. This project will expand the study to remove water hardness and soluble heavy metals like lead and chromium-6 without impairing the safety of drinking water. Also, the proposed technology will not require expensive water treatment facilities or extensive water pipe replacement. If combined with renewable solar power, it will be completely off the grid thus making the project eco-friendlier.
Results:
The project team will obtain the following information in optimizing the EP system using conductive concrete: 1) the optimum operating condition under batch and continuous flowing conditions, 2) system design parameters to treat extremely hard tap water, 3) heavy metal removal efficiency. Special care will be taken for data quantity and quality including redundant data collection and statistical analysis for data reliability.

CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
TITLE: Developing a tunable 3D Printed Membrane for Desalination
ABSTRACT:
New desalination technology(tunable 3D printed membrane) is proposed by professors from the UTRGV engineering school. The pore size of three elastic filaments printed to form a triangular stack (i.e. membrane) is pressed to change the opening by vertical pressure. At the right pore size, desalination is possible by placing pressurized seawater at one side of the membrane and allowing only fresh water pass through. It is expected to be fast-paced research and has great potential to be developed into a marketable product thus realizing a research enterprise and increasing research opportunities for the UTRGV.

CONGRANT.TITLE: BORDER 2020: US-Mexico Border Environmental Program RFP No. : SOLTA-C-19-013
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Project Objectives
The objective of the project is to provide technical, economic, and environmental information on various recycling methods of shredded scrap tires in quantified manner. A comprehensive literature review shall be conducted including the state-of-the-art, state-of-the-practice, and case examples of TDR aggregate. To understand the current conditions of scrap tire recycling, a survey shall be made for the engineers and local government employees in LRGV area. Based on the collected information, the project team shall compare the economic and environmental impacts of each recycling method through a systematic cost-benefit analysis and environmental evaluation.

CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Scrap tire chips will be tested as an alternative to coarse aggregate media in the septic tank drain field. This will help the U.S.-Mexico border region decide if it’s feasible to use scrap tires in place of expensive aggregate for the septic tank drain fields. Also, the contaminant removal capability of scrap tire chips will be tested to address its superior applicability to the onsite wastewater treatment like a septic tank. This project will ultimately promote sustainable materials and waste management and clean sites [Goal 3].

A water resource development from atmospheric air in Gulf of Mexico
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The atmospheric water is estimated to be enough to alleviate global water shortage. Currently US states including CA and TX are suffering from decreasing water resources. Since ocean air from the Gulf of Mexico is saturated with moisture, atmospheric moisture can be a sustainable alternative to provide water for arid local communities in South Texas. We have harvested atmospheric moisture from South Padre Island to test quality of collected water for its reuse and to learn about the feasibility of the proposed water resource development scheme. This project will showcase UTRGV’s continuous efforts for innovative and sustainable water resource development.

CONGRANT.TITLE: ISRP: A self-sustaining process to get fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: The project aims to explore a new process to get fresh water from oceans. The process is to be fully powered by the oceans themselves by means of the temperature gradient and waves. It does not use membranes to desalinate seawater. It does not produce brine either. Rather, it mimics the earth’s hydrologic cycle to a certain extent. Specifically, above an ocean surface warm air gains high humidity through natural solar heating. Below the ocean surface the water temperature naturally decreases with increasing water depth. By forcing the moisture-laden warm air to circulate through a cooling path down to the cold ocean at a certain depth, condensation occurs and fresh water is collected.  The air circulation is driven by ocean waves. With the help of winds, inexhaustible moisture-laden air can continuously move into the dehumidification site, making large-scale fresh water production possible.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Development of a Novel Nanoporous Fiber-Integrated Graphene Membrane for Reverse Osmosis Desalination
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
To address the fast growing population and clean water stresses in the lower Rio Grande
Valley (LRGV) regions in South Texas, the goal of this research is to develop a scalable and
energy-efficient porous graphene-carbon fiber polymeric composite membrane using the
Forcespinning® technology (given the industrial yield, promises low cost materials) for the next
generation of Reverse Osmosis (RO) membrane. This proposed membrane will have good
mechanical integrities because it naturally has nanopores due to the incomplete coverage between
the graphene sheets and the nanofibers. Three tasks and one educational task will be conducted
during the total 18 months of this project: Task-1, Fabrication of the porous nanofiber-integrated
graphene membrane using Forcespinning®; Task-2, Mechanical properties of the proposed
membrane; Task-3, Measurement of water quality after desalination using the proposed membrane;
Task-4, Educational plan. This proposed research will develop scalable and low cost graphenefiber
hybrid composite membrane, therefore it will significant reduce the energy input for the RO
process, by satisfying DWPR’s goal of “increasing water supplies by reducing the cost, energy
consumption, and environmental impacts of treating impaired and otherwise unusable waters.”
The requested fund will be used to support 0.25 month summer support (with 18% fringe benefits)
for all three PIs, two graduate assistantships (with 10% fringe benefits), and three undergraduate
scholarships. $5,600 will be requested to support faculty and students travel to Nano World
Conference 2019 and ASME IMECE 2019, $12,000 will be requested to purchase raw materials
and test supplies for membrane fabrication and water quality test, as well as ANSYS Mechanical
license. $1,200 will be used to support Dr. Yuanbing Mao as an advisor to review our experimental
data, quarterly reports and final report. Therefore the total direct cost is $101,584, the total indirect
cost is $35,025, and the total request fund is $137,409. UTRGV also commits $42,112 as nonfederal
cost share by releasing 10% of the three PIs’ workloads, and Nano Center at UTRGV will
also provide $5,000 as non-federal cost share for equipment use.
This project will be performed starting from October 1st, 2018 until March 31st, 2020, lasting
for 18 months in total, and one final report and five quarterly reports will be produced.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Life Cycle Cost Analysis (LCCA) of the Construction of a New Wastewater System for Smart Cities
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Water scarcity is a major concern worldwide. The recycling of wastewater has drawn much attention lately. Most wastewater produced is greywater, which does not have much contaminants and can be easily recycled using one treatment process. However, mixing greywater with blackwater requires nine treatment processes before the disposal of wastewater. This research focuses on the life cycle cost analysis of a novel smart wastewater system. In this research, we propose the construction two sewer lines: one dedicated to blackwater, and the other carries greywater. The research aims to assess the feasibility of the implementation of this new transforming wastewater system.

CONGRANT.TITLE: UTRGV Internal Seed Research Program (ISRP)
CONGRANT.SPONORG: Office of Research, Innovation, & Economic Development
CONGRANT.AWARDORG: The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
One of by-products of anaerobic digestion (AD) system is renewable biogas. As biogas production through AD has been increasing in US and Europe, there is unbent need for optimization AD system in terms of process stability, higher methane yields, and inhibition problems including high ammonia in feed waste. Biogas is usually consisted of 50 to 65% methane and it can be converted into energy and heat via combined heat and power (CHP) system. Due to technical limitation, CHP system can only accept cleaner biogas containing much less moisture, hydrogen sulfide and siloxane than untreated biogas and it necessitates expensive gas treatment equipment.

Biochar is a stabilized charcoal created by heating biomass under limited or no oxygen condition (pyrolysis). By the charring the biomass, much of the carbon becomes “fixed” into a more stable form that can minimize carbon dioxide emission to the atmosphere. In recent years, the potential use of biochars for soil amendment (Liang et al., 2008), long-term carbon storage (Lehmann, 2007), and contaminant removal (Mohan et al., 2014) has been receiving many attentions from scientists and funding agencies (e.g., USDA and NSF). Recently one of US national laboratories developed a novel biogas upgrade technology using biochar derived from organic wastes such as corn stover and woody material (Shen et al., 2015 and 2016). According to their research, AD system receiving biochars as additive produced biogas containing up to 90% methane and less than 5 ppm hydrogen sulfide, which can maximize the efficiency of the AD system. Porous structure and large surface area of biochar was found to sequester carbon dioxide and other impurities in biogas, thus improving biogas quality without additional downstream gas treatment. It was also claimed that biochar helped stabilize the digester performance by reducing ammonia toxicity and providing important minerals for microbes.

We propose a research to test the synergetic effect of biochar to AD system using biochar derived from citrus peel and palm tree waste, which are commonly available in the valley area. The proposed study will benefit wastewater treatment and renewable biogas energy facilities by achieving following:
1. Finding process limitations of proposed anaerobic digestion enhancement using biochar.
2. Providing data specific to the use of locally available biomass wastes as to economically enhance conventional waste treatment system and upgrade renewable biogas to pipeline quality.
3. Developing an alternative biogas upgrade technology that eliminates needs of expensive downstream biogas treatment equipment.

Proposed research will combine the expertise from two junior faculty members at CIVE and SEEMS. CIVE is one of the fast growing program in engineering and PI’s expertise on wastewater treatment will be combined with co-PI’s ongoing biochar research. With increasing regional/national emphasis on energy and environmental quality, this proposal will serve as a platform to accelerate the research productivity from both faculty members.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Sustainable Agricultural Use Of Treated Produced Water In Semi-Arid Areas
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
The overall objective of the project is to develop a sustainable crop production method in semiarid
regions by re-use of large amounts of oil and gas produced water with a novel energyefficient
Multi-Effect-Thermosyphon-Distillation (METD) unit. Continuous monitoring and
research on the influence of reclaimed irrigation on plant growth and soil health is made to
investigate the potential impacts on soil properties and crop yield caused by irrigation in
agriculture using the reclaimed water. The comprehensive plan spans all areas from acquiring of
the produced water to delivering it to growring suitable crops. The various steps include
identification and characterization of produced water resources in semi-arid areas of Oklahoma
and south Texas; pre-treatment of produced water using passive systems and aeration;
demonstration of the application of a novel energy-efficient and simple thermal treatment
system; optimization of the combination of produced and treated water for crop growth; a study
of the soil heath impact and crop growth effects with the use of recycled water; and periodic
meetings with local farmers and oil/gas industry personnel advocating the developed
methodology for furthering the use of our fresh water resources in sustained agricultural practice
and reducing the amount of fresh water used in the oil/gas industry during production. It is
expected that the water treatment plan developed in the course of this project will be useful in
the conversion of the major portion of about 20 billion barrel of annual produced water to fresh
water that can be used for food production.

CONGRANT.TITLE: An engineered hydrologic cycle for fresh water from oceans
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT: Two-thirds of the world’s population face severe water scarcity (Sci. Adv. 2, e1500323, ’16). Existing desalination technologies (e.g., membrane-based, thermal-based, etc.) have various drawbacks on scale up, energy consumption, water quality, and environmental impact (Water Res., 75, 164, ’15). Emerging technologies for collection of airborne water are limited to small-scale production (Science, 356, 430, ’17). Mother Nature feeds the globe with freshwater by extracting it from oceans through the hydrologic cycle (HC) – evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. We propose an engineering research project to engineer the HC at an ocean site for utility-scale freshwater production. Simply put, moist warm air over the ocean surface continuously enters a downward flow passage and reaches a certain water depth, where the air is naturally cooled by chilled ocean water and the airborne water is collected through condensation. The cold dry air then runs through an upward flow passage, escapes at the warm ocean surface, and recovers temperature and humidity. The uniqueness is on realizing a fully nature-powered engineered HC: winds to feed the site with inexhaustible moisture-laden air, waves to drive the air through the flow passage, the temperature gradient of the ocean water to provide cooling for condensation, and the solar energy to power humidity replenishment.

CONGRANT.TITLE: Texas Sea grant
CONGRANT.SPONORG: The Texas Sea Grant College Program
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Biogas production can support sustainable communities by reducing methane emissions, improving water quality, producing a local source of renewable heat, electricity and fuel, and strengthening the local economy by reducing energy costs and generating revenue. Biogas production by anaerobic digestion (AD) system has been proven to effectively stabilize high strength organic wastes if operated in a proper manner. In recent years, byproducts from the anaerobic treatment of organic waste (renewable biogas and fertilizer quality digestate) have been spotlighted due to their renewable, greenhouse gas reducing and eco-friendly characteristics.

It is common to see animal manures or sewage sludge as a feedstock for the AD system. Combining them with fish waste could be a sustainable feedstock in Texas Coastal Communities. Fish wastes have high valued organic carbon for methane production but also have limitation due to their high protein content (15-20 % of wet weight), which can be converted to ammonia nitrogen during the AD process resulting in a system upset by ammonia toxicity when excessively generated.

Biochar can enhance anaerobic digestion performance by achieving better biogas quality, greater ammonia toxicity suppression thus promoting better digester stability, and potentially enabling to treat higher organic wastes without increasing size of treatment tank. Biochar is a charcoal created by heating biomass under limited or no oxygen condition (pyrolysis) and it has been receiving attentions for soil amendment, long-term carbon storage, and contaminant removal. In this project, biochar produced from wasted sugarcane residue will be added to the AD system, so there will be less monetary investment requirement for real field application.

Overall objective of this project is to test the synergetic effect of biochar to a completely mixed AD system receiving fish wastes generated from Texas coastal communities. Phase 1 of this project will be carried out in batch AD systems treating primary sludge from a local wastewater treatment plant. During the first phase, multiple anaerobic batch reactors with different amounts of sugarcane biochar will be incubated at room temperature for 3 weeks. Phase I will determine optimum operational condition based on biogas generation, organic removal and process stability.

Phase 2 of this project will be performed in more controlled environment. Completely mixed anaerobic digestion system will be built and predetermined amount of biochar will be added to understand the changes in the system performance as per different operational environments determined from Phase I. Variations includes treatment temperature, organic loading rate, and substrate composition.

Based on the findings, we propose to upgrade conventional digestion system to codigestion system as the phase 3 of the study. Codigestion anaerobic digestion is the anaerobic waste treatment system treating combination of two or more organic wastes such as fish waste. Conventional AD system is not equipped to perform codigestion because high organic food loading can deter the stability of system performance. Biochar is claimed to help stabilize the digestion system by suppressing ammonia toxicity, from which the anaerobic codigestion system may benefit.

CONGRANT.TITLE: EREF Research Grant
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
Project Summary
The anaerobic digestion (AD) system has been proven to effectively stabilize organic wastes if operated in a proper manner. In recent years, byproducts from the anaerobic treatment of organic waste, namely renewable biogas and fertilizer quality digestate, have been spotlighted due to their renewable, greenhouse gas reducing and eco-friendly characteristics. Current research efforts in the AD system have been focusing on enhancing waste to energy conversion rate, advanced stabilization of anaerobic digestion processes, and downsizing the system without harming its organic removing performance. Proposed study fits in the current trend of anaerobic digestion study by aiming at all three major study objectives. Based on the previous laboratory scale batch studies (Shen et al., 2015 and 2016), biochar can enhance anaerobic digestion performance by achieving better biogas quality, greater ammonia toxicity suppression thus promoting better digester stability, and potentially enabling to treat higher organic wastes without increasing size of treatment tank. Biochar is a charcoal created by heating biomass under limited or no oxygen condition (pyrolysis) and it has been receiving attentions for soil amendment, long-term carbon storage, and contaminant removal (Mohan et al., 2014). In this project, we will produce biochars from wasted biomass so there will be less monetary investment requirement for real field application.

We propose a research to test the synergetic effect of biochar to a completely mixed AD system using biochar derived from citrus peel, palm tree waste, and arundo donax (giant reed) representing agricultural waste, garden waste, and invasive plant, respectively, common in the Rio Grande valley area, South Texas. The proposed study will benefit wastewater treatment and biogas production facilities by achieving following:
1. Finding process limitations of proposed anaerobic digestion enhancement using biochar.
2. Providing data specific to the use of locally available biomass wastes as to economically enhance conventional waste treatment system and upgrade renewable biogas to pipeline quality.
3. Developing an alternative biogas upgrade technology that eliminates needs of expensive downstream biogas treatment equipment.

Project Description
Phase 1 of this project will be carried out in batch type anaerobic digestion systems treating primary sludge from a local wastewater treatment plant. During the first phase, multiple anaerobic batch reactors with different amounts of biochars will be incubated at room temperature for 3 weeks. A tube furnace will be used to make the biochars at three different pyrolysis temperature (300, 450, and 600 °C) with 1-h heating time under nitrogen flow (Fig. 1). The produced biochar will be characterized for the physical and chemical properties. Phase I will determine optimum operational condition based on biogas generation, organic removal and process stability.

Phase 2 of this project will be performed in more controlled environment. Completely mixed anaerobic digestion system (Fig. 2) will be built and predetermined amount of biochar will be added to understand the changes in the system performance as per different operational environments determined from Phase I. Variations includes treatment temperature, organic loading rate, and substrate composition. Figure 2. Process Flow Diagram

Based on the findings, we propose to upgrade conventional digestion system to codigestion system as the phase 3 of the study. Codigestion anaerobic digestion is the anaerobic waste treatment system treating combination of two or more organic wastes such as food waste, agricultural waste, municipal sludge, etc. Conventional AD system is not equipped to perform codigestion because high organic food loading can deter the stability of system performance. Biochar is claimed to help stabilize the digestion system by suppressing ammonia toxicity, from which the anaerobic codigestion system may benefit.

CONGRANT.TITLE: EREF Research Grant
CONGRANT.ABSTRACT:
We propose to design and develop a hybrid process comprising a completely mixed mesophilic anaerobic codigestion of food and yard waste, and a self-regenerating catalytic process to remove the toxic organic pollutant from the liquid digestate. The simplified process diagram is shown in Fig.1. Due to mechanical limitations, a completely mixed system can efficiently mix only those wastes with less than 10% solids contents. Usual solids contents of high organic substrates such as food waste are much greater than 20% and dilution should accompany the codigestion of these substrates in the completely mixed system. Final liquid digestate is usually used for diluting feed waste but high ammonia in the liquid digestate may overload the system leading to system upset. In this regard, dilution water needs to be low in organic and toxic chemicals. The proposed catalytic chemical reaction can effectively remove organic pollutants and chemicals from the liquid digestate using renewable energy. In addition, catalyst can be synthesized with nanoporous biocompatible and sustainable materials. The proposed technology involves synthesis of an ideal nanostructured self-activated catalyst with or without quantum dot (QD) arrangement, and biocompatible functionalization of the supporting materials. This functional material would lead to the greatest enhancement of the catalytic cleaning kinetics of the toxic digestate. By modifying the nanoporous photoactive catalyst and/or QD arrangement (pure CdS, pure CdSe, or a mixture of CdS-CdSe) with or without organic/inorganic ligand, the noble metal-based dopant, and the catalyst functionalization (–OH, –COOH, etc.), we will extract the information necessary to determine the faster photocatalytic cleaning and transport kinetics. We propose to develop an efficient hybrid codigestion process with understanding of the underlying mechanisms that govern these photocatalytic processes.

Proposal Justification and Objective
The objectives of the project are to optimize the anaerobic codigestion system by synthesizing an efficient Quantum Dot (QD) (CdS, CdSe, Cds-CdSe etc.) and combining it with photoactive nanostructured hybrid-materials to prepare efficient, self-regenerating stable materials that will produce clean water for reuse/dilution, solid waste for safe disposal or agricultural use and bio-gas for energy applications (Fig. 2).
There are several advantages to incorporating QDs into photoactive semiconductor (such as TiO2, SiO2, etc.) materials. We propose a hybrid semiconductor supporting material for treatment and self-regeneration processes. First, QDs lower the bandgap of the composite semiconductor phase when compared to bare TiO2. QD-sensitized photoactive phase exhibits unique potential capability to produce quantum yields >1 by impact ionization (inverse Auger effect). Secondly, when a QD is combined with inorganic (or –organic) hybrid ligand, this leads to enhancement in short circuit current density and the ability to sustainably tune the stability of the electron-hole recombination process. The development of a biocompatible materials-based photoactive nanostructured support, which exhibits excellent optoelectronic properties toward stable electrocatalytic reactions, is especially suitable for enhanced photocatalytic decomposition performance in treatment of organic toxicants.
We expect the following objectives from the proposed study:
1. Development of a new anaerobic codigestion system with liquid digestate recirculation for feed waste dilution.
2. The treatment of liquid digestate with a catalytic chemical reaction, which uses green and renewable energy to protect our water system.
3. Optimization of operational data of a completely mixed anaerobic codigestion system treating high organic food waste and yard waste.
4. Performance data of mesophilic anaerobic codigestion system under different operational conditions including different feed sizing, feed pretreatment methods, and feed mixing ratio.
The proposed research can provide a new approach to codigestion for municipalities in which landfilling is the only economical choice for removing final digestate and there is a need for cost reduction in daily operation and maintenance.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: The effect of an aluminum addition to the single-stage thermophilic and mesophilic anaerobic digestion systems
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: World Academics Journal of Engineering Sciences
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Aluminum is widely used to remove soluble phosphorus in wastewater streams. However, its impacts on the performance of the anaerobic digestion systems are largely unknown. The recent Water Environment Research Foundation study (Document No. 03CTS9b) indicated that aluminum addition to the activated sludge system might improve the quality of the anaerobically digested sludge downstream. This study aimed to evaluate the benefits or drawbacks of additional aluminum to the performance of two anaerobic digestion systems that were operated under thermophilic (55 degrees Celsius) and mesophilic (37 degrees Celsius) conditions, respectively. The results indicated that aluminum addition up to 100 mg/L to the feed sludge could enhance solids removal in the mesophilic anaerobic digestion system while the solids removal in the thermophilic anaerobic digestion was adversely impacted by additional aluminum. Excess aluminum up to 300 mg/L did not deteriorate the stability of both digesters. Also, improved dewaterability was observed from the digested sludges of both systems with aluminum addition up to 300 mg/L to the feed sludge.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Mechanism of organic odor generation from thermophilically digested biosolids
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: In anticipation to generate more stabilized biosolids, thermophilic anaerobic digestion systems are widely used to destroy greater sludge organics thus making them less odorous. In this study, single-stage thermophilic (at 55℃) and mesophilic (at 37℃) anaerobic digesters were studied to compare organic removal efficiencies and sulfur-based odor generation from their biosolids. Although the thermophilic system removed about 9% more volatile solids than the mesophilic system, about 55 times more odorous organic sulfur compounds were measured from dewatered thermophilic biosolids. Different methanogenic species were found to be responsible for malodorous dewatered biosolids from the thermophilic anaerobic digester.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Impact of thermophilic aerobic pretreatment to the anaerobic digestion systems
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Multidisciplinary Sciences and Advanced Technology
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Aerobically pretreated sludge at a thermophilic temperature was digested in the following temperature phased anaerobic digestion system (TPAD) and single-stage mesophilic and thermophilic anaerobic digesters. Iron was added to the feed sludge to simulate an odor control at the field. A significant increase of volatile fatty acids and solids reduction were observed from the thermophilic aerobic pretreatment operated for 2.5 days retention time. Additionalsolids removal was also achieved in the subsequent anaerobic digesters resulting in 50% or greater volatile solids removal rate at a much shorter overall retention time of 14.5 days. The TPAD system removed the most % solids than single-stage thermophilic and mesophilic anaerobic digestion systems. However, biosolids from the single-stage mesophilic anaerobic digestion system were the most dewaterable and the least odorous after dewatering among three digestion systems. Excess iron did not suppress sulfur odor generation from the system with aerobic pretreatment.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Impact of iron on the digestion efficiencies and odor generation of the multi-stage anaerobic digestion system
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Iron addition to the feed sludge for single-stage mesophilic anaerobic digesters was reported to improve solids reduction efficiency and reduce odor generation from dewatered biosolids by a previous Water Environmental Research Foundation study (WERF Document No. 03CTS9b). In this study, a 4-stage anaerobic digestion system (6-day SRT for each stage) with a tapered temperature configuration (55oC, 49 oC, 46 oC, and 37 oC) was compared to both single stage mesophilic and thermophilic digesters for the same overall retention time. The single stage mesophilic system was operated with and without iron addition while the single stage thermophilic system was operated without iron addition. The data showed that for the multi-stage system, iron addition resulted in greater volatile solids destruction and less odorous dewatered biosolids compared to the system without iron addition. Also, improved biosolids dewaterability was observed from the multi-stage system with iron addition. For the single stage versus multi-stage systems, iron addition was less effective in solids reduction, odor and dewaterability from the single stage mesophilic anaerobic digestion system than from the multi-stage system. Single stage thermophilic system performed the worst in odor reduction and dewaterability.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: VS destruction and its impact on VOSC generation under thermophilic and mesophilic anaerobic digestion conditions
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Civil and Structural Engineering Research
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: Greater organic removal may result in less odorous sludge cake. Thermophilic (55℃) anaerobic digestion (TAD) and mesophilic (37℃) anaerobic digestion (MAD) were tested to understand if greater volatile solids reduction (VSR) could be related to less sulfur-based organic odor or volatile organic sulfur compounds (VOSCs) generation from dewatered and digested sludge. The TAD system removed 10% additional VS than the MAD system, which was reconfirmed by soluble and extractable biopolymer data. The TAD system held more soluble biopolymer than the MAD system while less extractable biopolymer was observed from TAD than MAD. However, greater organic solids removal did not result in lower odor in biopolymer cakes. Hydrogenotrophic methane formers might be responsible for less VOSC removal from thermophilically digested and dewatered sludge.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: A comparison of the temperature phased anaerobic digestion system to the single stage anaerobic digestion system
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: The performance of temperature phased anaerobic digestion system (TPAD) was compared to the performance of single-stage thermophilic and mesophilic anaerobic digestion systems. All 3 digestion systems were operated for the same overall retention time. Feed sludge was treated aerobically at thermophilic temperature for 2.5 days. The TPAD system removed greater solids than single-stage thermophilic and mesophilic anaerobic digestion systems. However, biosolids from the single-stage mesophilic anaerobic digestion system was the most dewaterable and the least odorous after dewatering among three digestion systems.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Lead in Drinking Water at a South Texas University
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: International Journal of Civil and Structural Engineering Research
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: With the Flint water crisis in Michigan, people concern more about the lead in the drinking water. Lead is a dangerous water toxin that the US Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) sets its Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) to be zero to prevent adverse health effects from lead poisoning. According to USEPA, buildings built before 1986 are likely to contain a lead piping system and drinking water running through those pipes may contain some level of lead. Also, worrisome level of lead was found from drinking water in public schools from US states (e.g. New York) due to the old piping system and insufficient maintenance on existing drinking water supply systems. A research team from a local Texas university measured lead in the school water fountains based on the facts that some buildings on campus are built before 1986 and year-long hot weather condition may accelerate lead leaching into the water pipelines thus resulting in higher lead level in drinking water. Test results showed that none of the water samples contained lead level greater than 15 ppb (or 15 μg/L), a Maximum Contaminant Level of lead action level in the drinking water set by USEPA. However, lead monitoring at other Texas public schools is warranted to protect Texas young citizens from lead poisoning from the drinking water.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Batch vs. Continuous Thermal Hydrolysis - Which is right for you?
INTELLCONT.PUBLISHER: Proceedings of the Water Environment Federation
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: A circular economy should benefit the consumer without producing waste or pollutants. In the wastewater industry, it is imperative we identify opportunities and develop solutions to harvest materials that appear to have little value and turn them into a valuable resource in order to realize the benefits of a circular economy. Thermal Hydrolysis is a proven cell lysing application for resource recovery in a sustainable and profitable manner from wastewater treatment plant. Two distinct thermal hydrolysis solutions have evolved, one a batch process and the other a continuous process. The two solutions are applicable in various configurations and each with unique features that will readily improve performance of existing anaerobic digesters or add considerably value to new digestion facilities. Often, the right solution for a wastewater treatment facility is not obvious. With energy cost on the rise and increase in population stressing the available natural resources, it is imperative that thermal hydrolysis efficiencies are improved to lower environmental impact. Numerous facilities across the globe have benefited from thermal hydrolysis, information from these facilities can be used to determine the ideal solution for most wastewater treatment plants. The design evolution, performance improvements, and lessons learnt over the past decade can also be used to assist wastewater treatment plants to fully realize the benefits of the circular economy.

INTELLCONT.TITLE: Nitrogen Removal in a Staged Anaerobic-Aerobic Sludge Digestion System
INTELLCONT.ABSTRACT: A mixture of primary and secondary municipal sludge was treated in the digestion system consisting of a first stage mesophilic anaerobic and a second-stage aerobic digester. The study was to monitor solids and nitrogen removal efficiencies under different operational conditions in the aerobic digester. In the first phase, the aerobic digester was batch fed under continuous aeration. More solids and ammonia were removed as the aerobic retention time increased. About 90% or greater ammonia was removed at 3 days or longer aerobic retention times. However, higher oxidized nitrogen was measured at the longer aeration times. In the second phase, the aerobic digestion system was operated for 3 to 5 days while continuously fed with anaerobically digested sludge under different intermittent aeration times. About 90% ammonia removal and low effluent oxidized nitrogen were achieved at 40 minutes of aeration over a 60-minute cycle at a 4-day retention time.

PRESENT.NAME: Transforming Our World Strategic Initiatives Symposium
PRESENT.TITLE: Renewable Water Resource from Gulf of Mexico
PRESENT.ABSTRACT: Globally more than two billion people lack clean water. Many renewable potable water production technologies have been tried, among which Atmospheric Water Generation involves extracting water from the ambient air. Currently 40% of the world’s population lives near the coast, where the hydrological cycle or water cycle, namely evaporation, condensation and precipitation, repeats. In the global hydrologic cycle evaporation from the water surface precipitates to produce rain and water vapor over the surface of the earth or plainly humidity, which is around 37.5 million billion gallons of water in total.  The accelerated economic and pollution growth in the RGV is increasing the demand for drinking water. The RGV shares the major water resource, Rio Grande river, with Mexico. As RGV is more urbanized, quantity and demand of drinking water will be an issue along with water quality deterioration. This project will be, water harvesting from sea water by extracting the evaporated water from the ocean air. It is the exploitation of one of the first stages for hydrologic cycle, evaporated water from the ocean that become localized humidity in the air. Initial analysis thus far, most of condensed oceanic air was slightly acidic, which indicates that sea water vapor has dissolved carbon dioxide that causes water to be acidic. The RGV is growing rapidly and the alternative water resource needs to be addressed quickly before it suffers from the shortage of potable water. Efficiency and water quality from dehumidification will be analyzed for this project to determine viability of the dehumidification as a dire resource of water for the RGV.
